title: Knowledge check: Machine-Learning Evaluation

questions.prompt: For “Machine-Learning Evaluation”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Use data separation and metrics that match the task; tuning on test data causes leakage. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Machine-Learning Evaluation” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Train, Validation, and Test Sets” as part of lesson 163. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Machine-Learning Evaluation” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Compare a simple baseline with a held-out estimate and identify one failure mode. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
